sources.title: Tiger Woods' apology: Full transcript
sources.speaker: Tiger Woods (prepared statement at TPC Sawgrass), transcript via CNN
sources.locator: Full transcript, opened and read end to end. Key passages: opening ('always tried to be a private person'); infidelity/entitlement paragraph; 'it's not what you achieve in life that matters'; role-model apology; 45 days inpatient therapy; privacy/children paragraph; Buddhism paragraph; return-to-golf paragraph; closing ask.
sources.excerpt: I want to say to each of you, simply, and directly, I am deeply sorry for my irresponsible and selfish behavior I engaged in. / And while I have always tried to be a private person, there are some things I want to say. / My behavior has caused considerable worry to my business partners. / I was unfaithful. I had affairs. I cheated. What I did is not acceptable. And I am the only person to blame. I stopped living by the core values that I was taught to believe in. I knew my actions were wrong. But I convinced myself that normal rules didn't apply. I never thought about who I was hurting. Instead, I thought only about myself. I ran straight through the boundaries that a married couple should live by. I thought I could get away with whatever I wanted to. I felt that I had worked hard my entire life and deserved to enjoy all the temptations around me. I felt I was entitled. Thanks to money and fame, I didn't have far -- didn't have to go far to find them. I was wrong. I was foolish. I don't get to play by different rules. / I once heard -- and I believe it is true -- it's not what you achieve in life that matters, it is what you overcome. Achievements on the golf course are only part of setting an example. Character and decency are what really count. Parents used to point to me as a role model for their kids. I owe all of those families a special apology. / For 45 days, from the end of December to early February, I was in inpatient therapy, receiving guidance for the issues I'm facing. / I have always tried to maintain a private space for my wife and children. They have been kept separate from my sponsors, my commercial endorsements / Buddhism teaches that a craving for things outside ourselves causes an unhappy and pointless search for security. It teaches me to stop following every impulse and to learn restraint. Obviously, I lost track of what I was taught. / When I do return, I need to make my behavior more respectful of the game. / I ask you to find room in your hearts to one day believe in me again.
sources.context: A scripted, televised statement read to an invited room of friends, staff, sponsors' representatives and pool reporters, with no questions taken. Delivered 84 days after the 2009-11-27 crash outside his home and 79 days after his 2009-12-02 written statement that problems 'shouldn't have to mean public confessions' (S03). The statement was a public-relations event as well as a confession; its self-analysis uses therapy vocabulary. It names no diagnosis: 'the issues I'm facing' is the only treatment language, so any 'sex addiction' label is not established by his words. The Globe and Mail transcript (S02) matches this wording; AJC's live-typed copy is rougher and should not be quoted. Edit stage (2026-10-04): the CNN copy returned HTTP 451 to several reviewers; the article now links the matching Globe and Mail copy (S02) and keeps CNN in citations. The room is described in S02 as friends, colleagues, supporters and foundation staff; the edit no longer asserts that sponsors' representatives were present.

sources.speaker: Wright Thompson (ESPN The Magazine), with named witnesses (John Brown, Ryan Zinke, Billy Helmers, Joe Grohman, Paul Fregia, Michael Jordan) and unnamed friends

Act II: Fort Bragg 2004, SEAL facility 2006, birthday skydive 2006-12-30, Michael Jordan passage, introvert/marketability passage, Halloween text, 'impersonation' and '30 seconds' narration; Jordan 'public shaming'/'Rabbit Ears'/'erase' passage; 'Woods' camp declined to comment' note (reopened 2026-10-04)
sources.excerpt: Narration: Seventy-seven minutes after touching down in Kansas, Tiger took off again for Orange County. / Narration: TWENTY-FIVE DAYS after he buried his father and 15 before the 2006 U.S. Open, Tiger went back to visit the Navy SEALs / Brown: 'Why are you here?' ... 'My dad,' Tiger said, explaining that Earl had told him he'd either end up being a golfer or a special operations soldier. / Brown: I definitely think he was searching for something. / Narration: He chose to spend Dec. 30, 2006 -- his 31st birthday -- in San Diego skydiving with SEALs. / Unnamed friend: Frankly, the real Tiger Woods isn't that marketable. There isn't a lot of money to be made off a guy who just wants to be left alone to read a book. / Unnamed friend: Tiger was a natural introvert, and the financial interest for him to be extroverted really drove a wedge in his personality. / Woods (text to Notah Begay about a Halloween costume): I'm going as a golfer known as Tiger Woods. / Narration: Talk to enough people who've met him and it starts to seem like he's doing an impersonation of what he thinks a superstar athlete is supposed to be. / Narration: People who meet him for 30 seconds love him, and people who spend several hours with him think he's aloof and weird, while people who hang around long enough to know him end up both loving him and being oddly protective. / Jordan: He has ... no companion. ... He's gonna have to trust somebody. / Fregia: In some respects, he became what he loathed about his father. / Zinke: Tiger Woods never got wet and sandy. / Narration: Tiger hated that his dad cheated on his mom and cried to his high school girlfriend about it. / Grohman (narration): worried that Tiger didn't have friends his own age until high school. His friends were Earl and Earl's old military buddies. / Narration: He worries that Tiger is so haunted by his public shaming that he obsesses over it, perhaps sitting up in the middle of the night reading all the things people write and say about him. / Narration: 'Rabbit Ears,' Michael calls him sometimes. He hears everything. For Tiger, this dwelling on old mistakes is a path to madness. / Jordan: That bothers him more than anything. ... It looms. It's in his mind. It's a ship he can't right and he's never going to. What can you do? The thing is about T-Dub, he cannot erase. That's what he really wants. He wants to erase the things that happened. / Narration: People who meet him for 30 seconds love him, and people who spend several hours with him think he's aloof and weird, while people who hang around long enough to know him end up both loving him and being oddly protective. / (Woods' camp declined to comment for this story.)
sources.context: Long-form reported feature (about 18 months), published ten years after Earl's death and after the scandal, so it builds a hindsight narrative. Woods did not participate. Many motive claims come from unnamed friends or SEALs; Brown's 'two paths' account is second-hand recall. 'Impersonation' and the '30 seconds' line are Thompson's narration, not testimony. Fregia was the first director of the Tiger Woods Foundation. Also establishes the birth date (31st birthday on 2006-12-30, so born 1975-12-30) and that Tiger grew up an only child of the marriage with few friends his age (per Navy course pro Joe Grohman). The 'He worries that Tiger is so haunted...' sentence is Thompson's paraphrase of Jordan's worry, and 'He hears everything' is Thompson's gloss on Jordan's nickname; only 'That bothers him more than anything ... He wants to erase the things that happened' is Jordan quoted directly. Jordan is a friend ('I love him so much that I can't tell him...').

sources.title: TEXT OF STATEMENT BY TIGER WOODS
sources.speaker: Tiger Woods (website statement), reproduced by The Press Democrat (AP)
sources.excerpt: I am deeply aware of the disappointment and hurt that my infidelity has caused to so many people, most of all my wife and children. / After much soul searching, I have decided to take an indefinite break from professional golf. I need to focus my attention on being a better husband, father, and person.
sources.context: Opened replacement for the geo-blocked CNN copy (S04). Written statement nine days after the December 2, 2009 privacy statement (S03); his first public use of the word infidelity.

sources.title: Tiger Woods taking break from golf, admits infidelity
sources.speaker: Jim Loney and Pascal Fletcher (Reuters), via Fox News
sources.excerpt: Woods' use of the word 'infidelity' apparently amounts to his first public admission ... amid claims by multiple women, in the weeks since his Nov. 27 auto accident, that they had affairs with him.
sources.context: Contemporaneous wire report. Used only to establish that the two weeks after the crash brought public claims by several women; the article does not repeat tabloid counts or names.

claims.claim: In his 2010-02-19 statement Woods explained the affairs in his own words: 'I convinced myself that normal rules didn't apply', 'I felt that I had worked hard my entire life and deserved to enjoy all the temptations around me. I felt I was entitled.'
claims.passage: I felt that I had worked hard my entire life and deserved to enjoy all the temptations around me. I felt I was entitled.
claims.inference: His own account links achievement to exemption: a lifetime of earned results bought a private reward and a suspension of rules. 'Convinced myself' is self-deception language. This supports a worth-through-achievement reading (Type 3's self-deceptive image) more than appetite for intensity as such.
claims.alternative: The statement was prepared, read after 45 days of inpatient therapy, and uses treatment vocabulary ('convinced myself', 'entitled'); it is his post-treatment public account, not a contemporaneous record of what he told himself in 2009. It may be the account therapy taught him to give. The edit says so in the opening and the 2010 section.

claims.claim: The same statement reframed his worth from results to character and asked for restored belief: 'it's not what you achieve in life that matters, it is what you overcome. Achievements on the golf course are only part of setting an example', apologized to families who 'used to point to me as a role model', to 'business partners', and closed: 'I ask you to find room in your hearts to one day believe in me again.'
claims.passage: He offered a new measure of worth: "it's not what you achieve in life that matters, it is what you overcome." He ended by asking the public to "one day believe in me again."
claims.inference: The repair he sought was in how he was seen: role model, belief, partners. Speaking of image restoration this directly fits a 3's concern with being regarded as valuable.
claims.alternative: Sponsors (Accenture, Gillette, AT&T had dropped or paused him) and an image-based fortune gave commercial reasons to ask for belief whatever his type; crisis PR norms dictate such language.

claims.claim: On 2009-12-02 Woods' written statement regretted unnamed 'transgressions', called privacy 'an important and deep principle', said 'Personal sins should not require press releases and problems within a family shouldn't have to mean public confessions', and said he must 'stick to that principle even though it's difficult'.
claims.passage: Five days later he posted a statement that regretted unnamed "transgressions" and set a boundary: privacy was "an important and deep principle," "Personal sins should not require press releases and problems within a family shouldn't have to mean public confessions," and he would "stick to that principle even though it's difficult"
claims.inference: His first, least commercially pressured response to exposure was a boundary, not image repair. The edit treats it as counterevidence to the picture-repair reading (closer to an Eight holding a line or a Five closing a door).
claims.alternative: Privacy statements are standard advice for public figures in a breaking scandal; it also admitted wrongdoing in general terms, so it was not a denial.

claims.claim: Former American Media CEO David Pecker testified under oath on 2024-04-26 that he bought the 2007 photos of Woods and buried them in return for Woods appearing in Men's Fitness. The draft states there is no public record of Woods' personal role and that his representatives may have made the deal; it does not name the woman photographed.
claims.passage: On April 26, 2024, testifying under oath in an unrelated trial, the publisher's former chief executive, David Pecker, said he had bought the photos and buried them in return for Woods appearing in the magazine
claims.inference: A costly, deliberate image trade: he supplied an idealized public image (fitness and marriage) to keep a contradicting one hidden. This is the clearest observed act of protecting an image rather than confronting a threat.
claims.alternative: Brand protection was worth tens of millions in endorsements, so his agents may have driven the decision; there is no evidence of Woods' personal role or words. Pecker's testimony came 17 years later in an unrelated trial. 'Blackmail' is a reporter's word, not a finding. Sensitive: name the other woman only as reported, if at all.

claims.claim: In his 2017 book Woods wrote: 'I probably came back too early from some of the surgeries, but I was single-minded in my desire to compete and my need for competition.'
claims.passage: "I probably came back too early from some of the surgeries, but I was single-minded in my desire to compete and my need for competition"
claims.inference: He names competing as a need, not just a preference, and accepts physical cost for it. Consistent with identity fused with performance.
claims.alternative: Elite athletes broadly describe competition as a need; career incentives, sponsor obligations and fear of decline explain early returns. Also fits an 8's refusal to yield to the body.

claims.claim: Steve Williams says he asked Woods three times during the 2008 U.S. Open whether to carry on and got 'F--- you, Stevie, I'm winning this tournament' each time.
claims.passage: His caddie, Steve Williams, asked three times whether carrying on was right and got the same reply: "F--- you, Stevie, I'm winning this tournament."
claims.inference: Overriding medical advice and his own caddie to win shows willpower and an extreme priority on winning the biggest events.
claims.alternative: This is the strongest single datum for Type 8 (defiance, dominance, denial of vulnerability). Haney and Williams both later fell out with Woods. Major titles also drove his legacy and earnings. Two witnesses with independent vantage points agree, which strengthens the fact but not the motive.

claims.claim: After winning the 1997 Masters by a record 12 shots, Woods rebuilt his swing; in How I Play Golf (2001) he wrote: 'I didn't see one flaw. I saw about 10 ... by my standard, I felt I had gotten away with murder.'
claims.passage: "I didn't see one flaw. I saw about 10," he wrote in _How I Play Golf_ (2001). "I had struck the ball great that week, but by my standard, I felt I had gotten away with murder."
claims.inference: Accepting a short-term slump after a record win to secure dominance every week. The stated goal is consistent results under pressure, not appearance. Repeated with Haney (2004) and later coaches.
claims.alternative: The perfectionist standard ('by my standard') supports Type 1; the mastery-and-control rationale supports Type 5; the impatience fits 8. A 3 reading has to treat the rebuild as investment in future winning, which is plausible but not unique.

claims.claim: In his 2022-03-09 Hall of Fame speech Woods credited his father ('Dad, who's not here, but who instilled in me this work ethic') with the rule: 'nothing's ever going to be given to you, everything's going to be earned ... you don't deserve it. You need to earn it. So that defined my upbringing. That defined my career' (ASAP Sports wording).
claims.passage: "nothing's ever going to be given to you, everything's going to be earned. If you don't go out there and put in the work ... one, you're not going to get the results, but two, and more importantly, you don't deserve it. You need to earn it. ... That defined my career"
claims.inference: He states a rule that ties deservingness to earned results, the same logic he used in 2010 to excuse himself ('worked hard ... deserved'). The repetition across 12 years and opposite contexts (confession vs celebration) is the strongest self-report thread for a worth-through-achievement motive.
claims.alternative: This is also a Type 1 moral rule about effort and fairness, and a widely shared athlete ethic shaped by Earl's military values and racial exclusion ('twice as good to be given half a chance', S14). The ASAP transcript (opened 2026-10-04) ties the clause to his father; Golf Channel's rendering differs slightly in wording.

claims.claim: Woods said in 2022: 'I made practicing so difficult, hurt so much, because I wanted to make sure that I was ready come game time. I hit thousands of balls, hands bleeding, aching, just so that I could play in a tournament.'
claims.passage: I hit thousands of balls, hands bleeding, aching, just so that I could play in a tournament
claims.inference: Self-imposed pain in service of being ready to compete; used in the edit against the Seven reading (decades of grinding practice).
claims.alternative: Fits 8 (toughness, pain tolerance), 1 (discipline) and Earl's 'train hard, fight easy' military code as learned practice rather than motive.

claims.claim: At the 2022 Open Woods said LIV players were 'just getting paid a lot of money up front and playing a few events' and asked 'What is the incentive to go out there and earn it in the dirt?'
claims.passage: His 2022 attack on LIV Golf, a rival league whose players, he said, were "getting paid a lot of money up front," shows only that he means it: "What is the incentive to go out there and earn it in the dirt?"
claims.inference: The earned-equals-deserving rule is sincerely held across contexts. The edit labels this as consistent with several types, not a discriminator.
claims.alternative: Institutional loyalty to the PGA Tour, where he spent his career, explains part of it; an Eight's contempt or a One's moral desert would produce the same words.

claims.claim: An unnamed friend told Wright Thompson: 'the real Tiger Woods isn't that marketable. There isn't a lot of money to be made off a guy who just wants to be left alone to read a book', and another said Woods 'was a natural introvert, and the financial interest for him to be extroverted really drove a wedge in his personality.'
claims.passage: "Frankly, the real Tiger Woods isn't that marketable. There isn't a lot of money to be made off a guy who just wants to be left alone to read a book." Another: "Tiger was a natural introvert, and the financial interest for him to be extroverted really drove a wedge in his personality."
claims.inference: Friends perceive a gap between a commercially produced public self and a private, quieter self. A split between performed image and inner self is central to the Type 3 hypothesis.
claims.alternative: Read straightforwardly, the private self described here (introverted, bookish, wanting to be left alone) is the strongest evidence for Type 5 with a commercially imposed persona. Unnamed sources; hindsight framing.

claims.claim: Asked by Notah Begay about a Halloween costume, Woods texted: 'I'm going as a golfer known as Tiger Woods.'
claims.passage: Woods texted: "I'm going as a golfer known as Tiger Woods."
claims.inference: His own joke treats 'Tiger Woods' as a costume, an awareness that the public figure is a role. Supports the image/self gap in C12.
claims.alternative: Thompson presents it as humor during a hard period. One joke cannot carry a motive claim.

claims.claim: Wright Thompson's narration (2016): talk to enough people who have met Woods 'and it starts to seem like he's doing an impersonation of what he thinks a superstar athlete is supposed to be.'
claims.passage: "it starts to seem like he's doing an impersonation of what he thinks a superstar athlete is supposed to be."
claims.inference: A reporter's synthesis of many interviews: the public persona is rehearsed and modeled on an idea of what a star should be.
claims.alternative: The same aloofness counts against a 3's usual charm and adaptiveness; it fits 5's detachment or 8's indifference to approval. Author narration, not testimony.

claims.claim: Rachel Uchitel said in HBO's 'Tiger' (2021) that Woods 'was sick of trying to hide who he was but he was so scared of the real Tiger not living up to the Tiger that everybody else thinks he is.'
claims.passage: "He was sick of trying to hide who he was but he was so scared of the real Tiger not living up to the Tiger that everybody else thinks he is"
claims.inference: If accurate, this names a fear of the real self failing the public image. That is close to the Type 3 core fear stated in plain language.
claims.alternative: Her interpretation, from a party with an interest in her own rehabilitation; sensitive. Do not lean on it without the independent support of C04, C12 and C13.

claims.claim: After Earl Woods died on 2006-05-03, Woods left Kansas 77 minutes after landing for the burial, visited a SEAL training facility 25 days after the burial and 15 days before the 2006 U.S. Open (where he missed his first major cut as a pro), told a SEAL his reason was 'My dad', and spent his 31st birthday (2006-12-30) skydiving with SEALs.
claims.passage: At the burial in Kansas, Thompson reported, Tiger took off again 77 minutes after landing. Twenty-five days after the burial and 15 days before the U.S. Open, he went back to visit Navy SEAL training. A SEAL, John Brown, asked why he was there. "My dad," Woods said, explaining that Earl had told him he would end up either a golfer or a special operations soldier. Woods missed the cut at that U.S. Open, and he spent his 31st birthday skydiving with SEALs
claims.inference: Grief channeled into his father's world and a dangerous alternative identity, at real career cost (coach objections, a missed cut). It suggests identity searching after losing his primary audience and model.
claims.alternative: This is the strongest behavior the 3 hypothesis does not explain neatly: an arena with no audience and no golf payoff. It fits an 8's appetite for intensity, a 6's identification with his father's code, or grief alone. (Zinke's 'never got wet and sandy' was cut at edit for length; S17 still records it.)

claims.claim: Woods described himself in 2006: 'I'm kind of the one who bottles things up a little bit and moves on, tries to deal with things in my own way.'
claims.passage: "I'm kind of the one who bottles things up a little bit and moves on"
claims.inference: Emotion is set aside for function and released only after the result. Consistent with a 3's suspended feelings in service of performance.
claims.alternative: Equally consistent with 5's compartmentalization, 8's guardedness against vulnerability, or Earl's explicit coaching not to let 'emotions get the better of you'.

claims.claim: After Charles P. Pierce's April 1997 GQ profile printed crude jokes Woods told in a limousine, Woods, then 21, said he was 'naive about the motives of certain ambitious writers'.
claims.passage: At 21, burned by a GQ profile that printed jokes he had told in a limousine, he blamed "the motives of certain ambitious writers"
claims.inference: An early reputational wound followed by a long era of controlled, bland media access. Protecting image by restricting access.
claims.alternative: Media guardedness is also standard advice for a young star with large endorsements, and fits 5's privacy. The source chain does not prove the GQ episode caused the change.

claims.claim: When Butch Harmon criticized his swing in 2004, Woods said Harmon 'doesn't really know what I'm working on ... and no one knows' and that friends should 'go right up to my face and say it.'
claims.passage: Woods said Harmon "doesn't really know what I'm working on" and added, "If you go say something like that, you go right up to my face and say it."
claims.inference: Read both ways in the edit: a face-to-face code (Eight) and an objection that criticism went to the media rather than privately (Three).
claims.alternative: The 'say it to my face' code is a classic Type 8 marker; the secrecy fits 5. A 3 reading treats it as protecting his public narrative ('I am close') during a slump, which Harmon called 'denial'.

claims.claim: In Gary Smith's 1996 Sports Illustrated profile, Earl Woods proclaimed: 'He is the Chosen One. He'll have the power to impact nations. Not people. Nations.' Tiger's reported reply ('This is my purpose. It will unfold.') is not used because only an unauthorized reproduction (S56) was opened.
claims.passage: In 1996 Earl told Sports Illustrated: "He is the Chosen One. He'll have the power to impact nations. Not people. Nations."
claims.inference: A parent publicly assigned the child an identity of world-historical achievement. Context for an identity built around performance, not evidence of the son's motive.
claims.alternative: Circumstance, not type: any child framed this way could internalize it. Earl was a self-described mythmaker ('Let the legend grow', S58). Slate (S70) independently quotes the SI line, and GQ 1997 (S26) records Earl's similar 'change the course of humanity' line.

claims.claim: In 2013, when Charlie was four, Woods said that if his children played golf there would be 'no lessons ... just have fun'.
claims.passage: In 2013, when Charlie was four, he said that if his children played golf there would be "no lessons"
claims.inference: A change of mind: he came to reproduce his father's method, which shows how fully he endorses the training that formed him.
claims.alternative: Could reflect Charlie's own choices and talent rather than Woods' motive. The 2013 account of Earl steering him away from golf conflicts with biographers' accounts.

claims.claim: Woods appeared on national television (The Mike Douglas Show) at age two, in 1978.
claims.passage: He had been in public view far earlier, on _The Mike Douglas Show_ at two, in 1978
claims.inference: He performed for an audience before he could choose to. Context for an identity built around being watched.
claims.alternative: Circumstance alone; a 5 or 8 child could have had the same upbringing. Who arranged the appearance is not documented in opened sources.

claims.claim: Woods said that as a junior 'I was not allowed in the clubhouses where all the other juniors were. The color of my skin dictated that. As I got older, that drove me even more', and that he put his shoes on in the parking lot and asked only where the first tee was and what the course record was.
claims.passage: "I was not allowed in the clubhouses where all the other juniors were. The color of my skin dictated that. As I got older, that drove me even more," Woods said in 2022. He put his shoes on in the parking lot and asked two questions: "Where was the 1st tee, and what was the course record."
claims.inference: Exclusion was converted into fuel for results; results were the answer to status denied.
claims.alternative: Racism is a real, external circumstance; this is resilience under discrimination, not proof of type. Also fits 8's defiance.

claims.claim: At the 2013 Masters Woods' own post-round account of dropping '2 yards further back' led to a two-stroke penalty rather than disqualification; he said he accepted the penalty and respected the committee's decision, and kept playing.
claims.passage: Neither does the 2013 Masters, where his own account of dropping "2 yards further back" led to a two-stroke penalty rather than disqualification. He said he would "accept the penalty and respect the Committees' decision" and kept playing
claims.inference: Candor (One-like) plus compliance with a sanctioned ruling; the edit says the episode does not settle the One question either way.
claims.alternative: He said he was unaware he had broken a rule; staying in the field followed the committee's ruling, so it is not evidence of defiance.

claims.claim: On 2017-05-29, a little over a month after his April 20, 2017 spinal fusion, Woods was arrested for DUI in Jupiter, Florida; he called it 'an unexpected reaction to prescribed medications' and said 'I expect more from myself, too.'
claims.passage: On May 29, 2017, a little over a month after spinal fusion surgery, Woods was arrested for DUI in Jupiter, Florida. He called it "an unexpected reaction to prescribed medications" and said, "I expect more from myself, too"
claims.inference: Self-managed medication during severe back pain; public framing shifted as facts emerged. 'I expect more from myself' is self-standard language.
claims.alternative: Sensitive medical/legal matter. Chronic pain and surgery are the main circumstantial explanation; this is not type evidence and must not be framed as character diagnosis.

claims.claim: Woods won the 2019 Masters after the 2017 fusion surgery and arrest.
claims.passage: He came back to win the 2019 Masters.
claims.inference: Context for the 2021 Everest quote about the post-fusion comeback.
claims.alternative: None material; a dated, completed result.

claims.claim: On 2021-02-23 Woods crashed near Rancho Palos Verdes; the LA County Sheriff said the primary cause was unsafe speed (84-87 mph in a 45 zone). No impairment evidence was found and no citation was issued; Woods said he was 'grateful for all the help I received.'
claims.passage: After a February 23, 2021, crash near Rancho Palos Verdes, California, which the sheriff attributed to unsafe speed, with no evidence of impairment and no citation
claims.inference: His public reply stressed gratitude and recovery, not the speed finding.
claims.alternative: An accident under investigation that found no impairment; no type inference should rest on it.

claims.claim: On 2026-03-27, three days after a TGL appearance, Woods was arrested on suspicion of DUI after a rollover crash on Jupiter Island, Florida. Per the sheriff's office and the arrest affidavit: breath test negative; he refused a urine test; two hydrocodone pills in his pocket; he told deputies he had been looking at his phone and changing the radio station.
claims.passage: On March 27, 2026, three days after a TGL match, he was arrested on suspicion of DUI after a rollover crash on Jupiter Island, Florida. According to the sheriff's office and the arrest affidavit, his breath test was negative, he refused a urine test and deputies found two hydrocodone pills in his pocket; he told them he had been looking at his phone and changing the radio station
claims.inference: Arrest-time allegations, all attributed to the sheriff/affidavit, later resolved by the 2026-09-02 plea (C69). Not type evidence.
claims.alternative: Allegations, not findings; the case ended in a plea to amended charges. His reported phone/radio account is his explanation at the scene, as recorded by deputies.
claims.review_trigger: Re-check if Woods returns to competition, makes a substantive public statement about his treatment, faces any further legal matter, or if any outlet corrects the 2026 arrest details.

claims.claim: Woods' first public appearance after the 2026 arrest, on 2026-06-23 as chair of the PGA Tour Future Competition Committee, was a prepared statement with no questions; his criminal case was pending until 2026-09-02, and ESPN gave no reason for the format.
claims.passage: His first appearance afterward, on June 23, 2026, as chairman of a PGA Tour committee, was a prepared statement with no questions
claims.inference: No type inference. The edit names pending-case legal caution as a sufficient explanation and removed the earlier 'unchanged since 2009' pattern claim. Removed from type_hypothesis.for_claim_ids.
claims.alternative: Ordinary legal caution during a pending prosecution; also consistent with Five-style withdrawal.
claims.review_trigger: Re-check when Woods next gives an unscripted interview or press conference, or if his PGA Tour committee or board role changes.

claims.claim: In 2010 Woods described Buddhism, 'which my mother taught me at a young age', as teaching him 'to stop following every impulse and to learn restraint'.
claims.passage: "which my mother taught me at a young age," which "teaches me to stop following every impulse and to learn restraint."
claims.inference: Doctrine meant for everyone, so weak type evidence; the problem it names is appetite, which an Eight reading absorbs more easily. No longer counted as a pillar of the Eight case.
claims.alternative: Religious and therapy vocabulary in a scripted statement; it says nothing distinctive about motive.

claims.claim: Steve Williams wrote that Woods would 'flippantly toss a club in the general direction of the bag' and had a 'habit of spitting at the hole if he missed a putt'.
claims.passage: Williams wrote that Woods would "flippantly toss a club in the general direction of the bag" and had a "habit of spitting at the hole if he missed a putt"
claims.inference: On-course temper was visible and recognized by Woods himself. Image management was not total.
claims.alternative: Counter to a pure 3 reading (a 3 usually polishes visible conduct); fits 8 or 1 anger. Williams has animus and book incentives, but Woods' own line corroborates the substance.

claims.claim: In his first interviews after the scandal (2010-03-21) Woods said therapy meant 'stripping away denial and rationalization'.
claims.passage: A month later he said therapy meant "stripping away denial and rationalization"
claims.inference: Supports the edit's point that the 2010 self-justification is phrased in treatment vocabulary.
claims.alternative: He may be describing real insight; vocabulary origin does not make the account false.

claims.claim: Woods said in 2024 that his daughter Sam has 'a negative connotation to the game, because when she was growing up, golf took Daddy away from her.'
claims.passage: Sam has "a negative connotation to the game, because when she was growing up, golf took Daddy away from her"
claims.inference: Names a family cost of his career.
claims.alternative: Ordinary travel cost of a touring athlete.

claims.claim: Hank Haney said Woods 'wanted to be a Navy SEAL. For sure that was on his list'; agent Mark Steinberg said Haney twisted Woods' 'high respect for the military'.
claims.passage: Haney later said, "He wanted to be a Navy SEAL. For sure that was on his list"; Woods' agent, Mark Steinberg, said Haney had twisted Woods' "high respect for the military"
claims.inference: At his peak, he seriously pursued an identity outside golf tied to his father.
claims.alternative: Contested by his camp; sources have incentives (Haney's book) or are anonymous. Supports the unexplained-behavior column rather than any type.

claims.claim: Michael Jordan told Thompson that Woods has '... no companion' and is 'gonna have to trust somebody', framed as worry about his happiness.
claims.passage: Jordan's worry was isolation: Woods has "no companion," he said, and "He's gonna have to trust somebody."
claims.inference: A friend's concern about isolation and trust; presented as concern, not as evidence of coldness.
claims.alternative: Friend's speculation. Low trust fits 5, 6 and 8 as much as 3. (Fregia's line and the father-infidelity detail were cut at edit as gratuitous.)

claims.claim: At 14 1/2 the family took out a second mortgage so Woods could play the AJGA tour; Golf Channel reported he paid it off with his first Titleist deal.
claims.passage: At 14 1/2, the family took out a second mortgage so he could play the national junior tour; Golf Channel reported that he paid it off with his first Titleist deal.
claims.inference: Loyalty and repayment to family; achievement as provision.
claims.alternative: Fits many types; mainly a humanizing detail.

claims.claim: In his 2017 memoir The 1997 Masters: My Story, Woods wrote of his ex-wife, Elin Nordegren: 'My dishonesty and selfishness caused her intense pain. My regret will last a lifetime.'
claims.passage: "My dishonesty and selfishness caused her intense pain. My regret will last a lifetime."
claims.inference: Sustained ownership of the betrayal seven years later.
claims.alternative: Curated memoir voice.

claims.claim: Eldrick Tont 'Tiger' Woods was born 1975-12-30 in Cypress, California.
claims.passage: Eldrick Tont "Tiger" Woods was born on December 30, 1975, in Cypress, California
claims.inference: Factual metadata.
claims.alternative: Wikipedia is tertiary; the birth date is independently implied by Thompson's report that 2006-12-30 was his 31st birthday (S17). Birthplace rests on Wikipedia only.

claims.claim: In his 2022 Hall of Fame speech Woods recounted sneaking onto the Navy Golf Course at 8 via 'The Ditch', taught by his Green Beret father to 'grab a piece of foliage, cover yourself up, listen for noise. If you hear anybody coming, lay still ... Part sniper', then playing with Earl until dark.
claims.passage: In the Hall of Fame speech, Woods explained how he got onto the Navy Golf Course as an underage 8-year-old. His mother dropped him at the entrance, and he slipped into a ditch on the side the clubhouse couldn't see. His father, "a former special forces and a Green Beret," had "taught me how to always grab a piece of foliage, cover yourself up, listen for noise. If you hear anybody coming, lay still." The room laughed. "Part sniper." When Earl's cart came by after work, they played until dark
claims.inference: A self-told childhood story of hiding unseen until it was time to play; the draft labels the link to his later guardedness as its own reading.
claims.alternative: A humorous anecdote told 38 years later in a celebratory setting; it describes Earl's military habits and a practical way to play underage, not a motive.

claims.claim: Author interpretation: the Ditch story previews a recurring pattern of concealment until performance.
claims.passage: It is a funny story, and an early version of a skill that returns in this profile: staying out of sight until it is time to play.
claims.inference: Thematic link between the childhood anecdote and the later guarded public persona.
claims.alternative: Could be over-reading a funny, practical story; the draft presents it as the profile's framing, not as evidence of type.

claims.claim: Golf Channel reported Woods was slated to speak for seven minutes at the 2022 Hall of Fame induction and spoke for nearly 17, without notes or a teleprompter.
claims.passage: Slated to speak for seven minutes, he spoke for nearly 17, without notes
claims.inference: Sets the unscripted context for the speech quotes.
claims.alternative: Reporter's account; timing approximate ('nearly 17').

claims.claim: Author interpretation linking the 2010 self-justification and the 2022 speech: the same earned-equals-deserving rule.
claims.passage: It is the same rule both times: work earns results, and results make you deserving.
claims.inference: The central thread of the profile: the logic that built the career also supplied the 2010 excuse.
claims.alternative: Shared vocabulary could be coincidence or a common athlete ethic; the 2010 statement was scripted with advisers. The draft keeps both quotes verbatim so readers can judge the parallel.

claims.claim: In the 2010-02-19 statement Woods said: 'I convinced myself that normal rules didn't apply.'
claims.passage: In 2010 it explained an exemption: "I convinced myself that normal rules didn't apply."
claims.inference: Self-deception language tied to the earned-exemption logic of C01.
claims.alternative: Scripted statement with therapy vocabulary; also readable as Eight-style rule defiance.

claims.claim: The draft's type thesis: Type 3 at medium confidence, Type 8 strongest alternative, Type 5 serious second.
claims.passage: Tiger Woods most likely fits Enneagram Type 3, the Achiever, at medium confidence.
claims.inference: Summarizes the type_hypothesis: the deserving rule across contexts plus image repair when picture and private reality diverged.
claims.alternative: Type 8 explains the 2008 U.S. Open, temper and the self-described craving; Type 5 explains the introversion and privacy. Confidence stays medium.

claims.claim: In 2007 Woods appeared on a Men's Fitness cover with a 12-page story about his diet, workout regimen and marriage while the Enquirer's photos went unpublished; the NY Post and WSJ reported the arrangement after the 2009 scandal and American Media denied it at the time.
claims.passage: Woods instead appeared on the cover of Men's Fitness with a 12-page story "about his diet, workout regimen and marriage." The New York Post and The Wall Street Journal reported the arrangement after the 2009 scandal broke, and the Enquirer's publisher denied it
claims.inference: The observable image trade at the center of the Three argument.
claims.alternative: Woods' personal role is undocumented; agents may have arranged it for commercial reasons.

claims.claim: Hank Haney recalls that while the doctor showed the MRI, Woods was 'not really listening' and then said 'I'm playing the U.S. Open and I'm going to win.'
claims.passage: His coach, Hank Haney, remembered Woods "not really listening" as a doctor went through the MRI, then looking up: "I'm playing the U.S. Open and I'm going to win."
claims.inference: Overriding medical information to pursue a major title.
claims.alternative: Haney later fell out with Woods; recalled ten years on. Strong Type 8 datum.

claims.claim: Before the 2008 U.S. Open, with a 2007 ACL rupture he had played on and a new double stress fracture of the left tibia, Woods recalled that 'they were saying I was pretty much done for the year' and that he replied 'Ah, I don't know about that.'
claims.passage: Woods recalled: "From there, they were saying I was pretty much done for the year. I said, 'Ah, I don't know about that.'"
claims.inference: His own account confirms he set aside medical judgment to chase majors.
claims.alternative: Retrospective self-report in an anniversary oral history; consistent with Haney's and Williams' accounts. Fits Type 8 defiance as well as Type 3 priority on titles.

claims.claim: Butch Harmon says he wanted Woods to take a year over the 1997-98 swing rebuild, but 'that's not Tiger Woods. He wanted to do it all right now.'
claims.passage: His coach, Butch Harmon, wanted to go slowly: "But no, that's not Tiger Woods. He wanted to do it all right now."
claims.inference: Impatience for mastery after a record win.
claims.alternative: Decades-later recall; impatience fits Type 8 as readily as Type 3.

claims.claim: Thompson's narration describes three stages: people who meet Woods for 30 seconds love him; people who spend several hours with him find him aloof and weird; people who know him long love him and are oddly protective.
claims.passage: "People who meet him for 30 seconds love him, and people who spend several hours with him think he's aloof and weird, while people who hang around long enough to know him end up both loving him and being oddly protective." The first is what a Three predicts; the second is not.
claims.inference: Brief-contact charm fits a Three; the lapse after hours does not.
claims.alternative: Reporter's synthesis, not testimony; aloofness also fits Five or ordinary celebrity fatigue.

claims.claim: Golf Channel's Ryan Lavner (2022) called Woods 'one of the most guarded athletes in history'.
claims.passage: He became, in Golf Channel's 2022 phrase, "one of the most guarded athletes in history," though a young star with large endorsements had plenty of reasons to go quiet.
claims.inference: Long-run media guardedness.
claims.alternative: Commercial advice to a young star explains guardedness; causation from the GQ episode is not established, as the draft states.

claims.claim: In 2004 Woods said of his swing work: 'he's never asked me and I've never talked to him about it and no one knows.'
claims.passage: the secrecy about his swing ("no one knows," he said in 2004)
claims.inference: Secrecy about process, cited as Type 5 evidence.
claims.alternative: Protecting a work in progress from a TV critic is ordinary competitive caution.

claims.claim: In July 2006 Woods won the Open at Royal Liverpool, his first major after Earl's death and after his first missed major cut as a pro, broke down, and said 'I wish he could have seen this one last time.'
claims.passage: That July he won the British Open at Royal Liverpool, his first major since his father's death. A month earlier, after the SEAL detour described below, he had missed his first major cut as a professional. He broke down after the win: "I wish he could have seen this one last time"
claims.inference: Emotion released after the result.
claims.alternative: Ordinary grief; S60 renders the quote differently ('one more time'); the draft uses The Open's wording (S61).

claims.claim: In December 2022 Woods described testing his son Charlie with Earl-style mental pressure: 'if I can get into his head, that means someone else can get in his head ... That's what my dad believed in. You've got to be willing to take it.'
claims.passage: By December 2022 he was testing Charlie the way Earl had tested him: "if I can get into his head, that means someone else can get in his head. ... That's what my dad believed in. You've got to be willing to take it."
claims.inference: A change of mind from 2013's 'no lessons': he came to reproduce his father's method.
claims.alternative: May reflect Charlie's own choices and talent rather than Woods' motive.

claims.claim: The 2017 toxicology report found five drugs (hydrocodone, hydromorphone, alprazolam, zolpidem, THC); Woods said he had been treating back pain and sleep problems on his own and that 'it was a mistake to do this without medical assistance'; he entered a diversion program and prosecutors said he would plead guilty to reckless driving.
claims.passage: Toxicology found five drugs, including painkillers, sleep medication and THC. He said he had been treating back pain and sleeplessness on his own, "a mistake to do this without medical assistance," and entered a diversion program; prosecutors said he would plead guilty to reckless driving
claims.inference: Woods' own explanation ties the 2017 arrest to self-managed medication after surgery.
claims.alternative: Self-report about cause; NBC reports the plea as expected (October 2017), and the article says only that prosecutors said he would plead guilty.

claims.claim: In November 2021 Woods said: 'After my back fusion, I had to climb Mount Everest one more time. I had to do it, and I did. This time around, I don't think I'll have the body to climb Mount Everest, and that's okay.'
claims.passage: "After my back fusion, I had to climb Mount Everest one more time. I had to do it, and I did. This time around, I don't think I'll have the body to climb Mount Everest, and that's okay."
claims.inference: A stated loosening of identity from competition; 'had to' frames the 2019 comeback as compulsion.
claims.alternative: GOLF.com relay of the Golf Digest interview (original S69 not opened); behavior after 2021 partly contradicts it.

claims.claim: Woods was competing in TGL in March 2026, including a match on 2026-03-24.
claims.passage: In March 2026 he was competing in TGL, a team league
claims.inference: Behavior partly contradicts the 'that's okay' statement.
claims.alternative: Business roles and the desire to play a few events explain returns without any identity claim. The draft does not list every 2022-2024 start.
claims.review_trigger: Re-check if Woods competes again; add the latest appearance only if it changes the argument.

claims.claim: On 2026-09-02 Woods resolved the case by plea to an amended charge of reckless driving with a five-year driver's license suspension; ABC reports no contest and CBS reports guilty. He had initially pleaded not guilty.
claims.passage: On September 2, 2026, he pleaded to an amended charge of reckless driving, with a five-year license suspension; outlets differ on whether the plea was guilty or no contest
claims.inference: Legal resolution of the 2026 arrest.
claims.alternative: Outlets conflict on plea type (no contest vs guilty), so the draft says only 'plea deal on reduced charges'.
claims.review_trigger: Re-check if court records or a correction specify the plea type (no contest vs guilty) or if the license suspension terms change.

claims.claim: Woods initially pleaded not guilty, and on 2026-03-31 said he was 'stepping away for a period of time to seek treatment and focus on my health'.
claims.passage: He pleaded not guilty, said he was "stepping away for a period of time to seek treatment and focus on my health"
claims.inference: Controlled written disclosure with a privacy request.
claims.alternative: Standard legal and medical caution during a pending case.
claims.review_trigger: Re-check if Woods makes a further statement about his treatment or health.

claims.claim: A judge allowed Woods to leave the U.S. for an 'intensive, highly individualized and medically integrated program', and he told the PGA of America he would not captain the 2027 U.S. Ryder Cup team.
claims.passage: received a judge's permission to be treated abroad and declined the 2027 U.S. Ryder Cup captaincy
claims.inference: Withdrawal from public roles during treatment.
claims.alternative: Institutional communication; no direct Woods quote on the captaincy.
claims.review_trigger: Re-check if Woods is named to any future Ryder Cup or PGA Tour role.

claims.claim: Woods' 2010 statement said: 'When I do return, I need to make my behavior more respectful of the game.'
claims.passage: Still, Woods said in 2010 that he needed "to make my behavior more respectful of the game," which fits the broader reports without confirming Williams' details.
claims.inference: A general 2010 pledge consistent with broad reports of his temper; it does not confirm the specific claims in Williams' 2015 book.
claims.alternative: Generic accountability language in a scripted statement.

claims.claim: Woods has 82 PGA Tour wins (tied for the record) and 15 major championships, the 15th at the 2019 Masters.
claims.passage: He has 82 PGA Tour wins, tied for the record, and 15 major championships, the 15th at the 2019 Masters
claims.inference: Factual metadata.
claims.alternative: Record counts change only if he wins again.
claims.review_trigger: Re-check win totals if Woods records another PGA Tour or major win.

claims.claim: Earl Woods died 2006-05-03; Kultida Woods died 2025-02-04; Woods' children are Sam and Charlie.
claims.passage: His father, Earl, died on May 3, 2006, and his mother, Kultida, died on February 4, 2025. He has two children, Sam and Charlie.
claims.inference: Factual metadata.
claims.alternative: Kultida's reported age varies by outlet, so the draft omits it.

claims.claim: Metadata birth_date: 1975-12-30.
claims.inference: Factual metadata.
claims.alternative: Derived independently from S17 (31st birthday on 2006-12-30).

claims.claim: Metadata birth_place: Cypress, California, U.S.
claims.passage: Cypress, California, U.S.
claims.inference: Factual metadata.
claims.alternative: Single tertiary source; check against a primary biography if challenged.

claims.claim: Author interpretation: the earned-equals-deserving rule functioned in 2010 as a self-granted exemption.
claims.passage: The rule that built the career had become a license.
claims.inference: Connects the 2010 self-justification to the career rule.
claims.alternative: The 2010 wording came from a scripted statement shaped by advisers and therapists; the draft notes that commercial pressure explains part of the statement.

claims.claim: Author interpretation: the crisis sequence (2007 trade, December 2009 boundary, February 2010 apology) is consistent with a Three but does not separate Three from Eight, because the 2007 deal is not shown to be Woods' own act and the 2010 apology is what almost anyone with that much at stake would do.
claims.passage: The obvious test, what he did when the picture and the private reality came apart, can't separate a Three from an Eight on its own.
claims.inference: Demotes the former discriminator to consistent-but-confounded evidence, as critic-01 and enneagram-01 asked.
claims.alternative: Some readers will still see the 2010 'believe in me again' plea as image-first; the article lets them, without counting it as decisive.

claims.claim: Author interpretation against Type 5: appetite (the 2009 'temptations' self-account) and preoccupation with public commentary (Jordan via Thompson) cut against a Five's minimized needs and detachment; playing majors is the job and does not discriminate.
claims.passage: A Five keeps needs small; Woods "deserved to enjoy all the temptations around me." A Five detaches from what strangers think; Jordan worries about a man who can't stop reading it.
claims.inference: Replaces the draft's 'largest stage' argument, which reviewers showed does not discriminate.
claims.alternative: A Five under stress can act out appetites; the Jordan account is one friend's worry, relayed by one reporter.

claims.claim: Thompson reported, via Navy course pro Joe Grohman, that Woods had few friends his own age until high school; his friends were Earl and Earl's old military buddies.
claims.passage: Thompson also reported that until high school his friends were Earl and Earl's old military buddies.
claims.inference: Context for the SEAL identification with his father's world.
claims.alternative: Second-hand recollection; does not establish motive.

claims.claim: Lavner observed that in the 17-minute Hall of Fame speech Woods made only one passing mention of his life and career this century.
claims.passage: For 17 unscripted minutes, Golf Channel's Ryan Lavner noted, Woods made only one passing mention of his life and career this century: "Nothing about the Tiger Slam. Nothing about the majors. Nothing about the soaring highs. The scandals."
claims.inference: The speech centered on upbringing and earning rather than achievements.
claims.alternative: Reporter's characterization of an unscripted speech.

claims.claim: Sam Woods introduced her father at the 2022 induction, saying 'We didn't know if you'd come home with two legs or not.'
claims.passage: His daughter, Sam, introduced him: "We didn't know if you'd come home with two legs or not"
claims.inference: Family cost of the 2021 crash.
claims.alternative: Celebratory setting.

claims.claim: Woods closed the Hall of Fame speech: 'I didn't get here alone ... This is an individual award, but it's actually a team award. All of you allowed me to get here.'
claims.passage: "I didn't get here alone." Then: "This is an individual award, but it's actually a team award. All of you allowed me to get here."
claims.inference: The draft reads this as a rare loosening of the earning rule.
claims.alternative: Customary induction-speech gratitude; the draft labels its reading as interpretation.

claims.claim: Woods crashed his car outside his Isleworth home on 2009-11-27.
claims.passage: On November 27, 2009, Woods crashed his car outside his home.
claims.inference: Start of the 2009 exposure.
claims.alternative: No further detail needed.

claims.claim: In the 2010-02-19 statement Woods admitted affairs, disclosed 45 days of inpatient therapy for 'the issues I'm facing' (no diagnosis named), cited 'considerable worry to my business partners', and apologized to families who had pointed to him as a role model.
claims.passage: "I was unfaithful. I had affairs. I cheated," he said on February 19, 2010. He had spent 45 days in inpatient therapy for what he called only "the issues I'm facing." He acknowledged "considerable worry to my business partners" and apologized to the families whose parents "used to point to me as a role model for their kids."
claims.inference: The repair sought is in standing: partners, role-model status, belief.
claims.alternative: Crisis-PR norms and sponsors in the room shape such language; no diagnosis should be inferred.

claims.claim: In 2007 the National Enquirer obtained photographs of Woods with another woman, and they were not published.
claims.passage: In 2007, the National Enquirer obtained photographs of Woods with another woman. The photos never ran.
claims.inference: Precondition of the 2007 trade.
claims.alternative: The woman is not named in the draft.

claims.claim: Metadata description: Woods used 'deserve' in his 2010 self-justification and his 2022 Hall of Fame speech.
claims.passage: Tiger Woods used one word to explain his affairs in 2010 and his career in 2022: deserve.
claims.inference: Metadata summary of the central thread.
claims.alternative: 'Explain his affairs' compresses 'deserved to enjoy all the temptations around me'.

claims.claim: FAQ: Woods played the 2008 U.S. Open on a torn ACL and two stress fractures against medical advice and told his caddie he was winning.
claims.passage: He played the 2008 U.S. Open on a torn ACL and two stress fractures against medical advice and told his caddie he was winning.
claims.inference: Summarizes the Type 8 case in metadata.
claims.alternative: 'Against medical advice' is supported by his own account that doctors said he was 'pretty much done for the year'.

claims.claim: FAQ: unnamed friends described Woods to Thompson as 'a natural introvert' and as someone who 'just wants to be left alone to read a book'; he has been secretive about his swing work.
claims.passage: One friend told ESPN's Wright Thompson that Woods was "a natural introvert," another that he "just wants to be left alone to read a book," and he has been secretive about his methods.
claims.inference: Summarizes the Type 5 case in metadata.
claims.alternative: Unnamed sources.

claims.claim: FAQ summary of the 2010 statement's apologies and closing request.
claims.passage: He acknowledged worry he had caused his business partners, apologized to families who had seen him as a role model, and asked the public to "one day believe in me again."
claims.inference: Metadata restatement of C02/C87.
claims.alternative: Scripted statement.

claims.claim: Author framing of the Uchitel testimony: it resembles what unnamed friends told Thompson and Woods' own Halloween joke, but that is resemblance, not independent corroboration.
claims.passage: It echoes what unnamed friends told one reporter and Woods' own costume joke: resemblance, not independent proof.
claims.inference: Limits reliance on an interested party's psychological claim; the 2007 trade is no longer offered as corroboration.
claims.alternative: The convergence may reflect a shared hindsight narrative after 2009.

claims.claim: Type 1 is weaker but not ruled out: 'core values' and 'by my standard' support it, and a One under strain can grant a private exemption, so 'normal rules didn't apply' does not exclude it.
claims.passage: Type 1 is weaker but not ruled out. He spoke of "core values" and judged his swing "by my standard," and a One under strain can grant himself a private exemption, so "normal rules didn't apply" doesn't settle it.
claims.inference: The deciding consideration against One is where the distress lands (C95), not the rule exemption.
claims.alternative: Standards talk in a scripted apology is weak evidence either way.

claims.claim: Thompson (2016) reports Michael Jordan's worry that Woods is 'so haunted by his public shaming that he obsesses over it, perhaps sitting up in the middle of the night reading all the things people write and say about him'; Jordan's nickname for him is 'Rabbit Ears' ('He hears everything', Thompson's gloss); Jordan, quoted directly: 'That bothers him more than anything ... It looms. It's in his mind ... He wants to erase the things that happened.'
claims.passage: Thompson's 2016 feature reports that his friend Michael Jordan "worries that Tiger is so haunted by his public shaming that he obsesses over it, perhaps sitting up in the middle of the night reading all the things people write and say about him." Jordan sometimes calls him "Rabbit Ears," Thompson writes: "He hears everything." "That bothers him more than anything," Jordan said. "It looms. It's in his mind. ... He wants to erase the things that happened."
claims.inference: The incentive-independent observation the type call now rests on: six years after the apology, a close friend describes sustained preoccupation with public judgment and a wish to erase the record. An Eight usually stops caring what strangers think; a Five detaches from commentary; a One's torment is usually the inner critic.
claims.alternative: One friend's account, partly Thompson's paraphrase and gloss; Woods' camp declined to comment. Rumination also fits Six-style anxiety or ordinary shame after a public humiliation. Jordan's 'That' may refer to his old mistakes generally rather than to what is said about them.

claims.claim: On 2009-12-11, after reports by several women of affairs with him, Woods admitted 'infidelity' in a written statement and announced 'an indefinite break from professional golf'.
claims.passage: On December 11, after two weeks of reports about women who said they had been involved with him ([Reuters via Fox News, December 11, 2009](https://www.foxnews.com/sports/tiger-woods-taking-break-from-golf-admits-infidelity)), he admitted "infidelity" in writing and announced "an indefinite break from professional golf"
claims.inference: The privacy boundary of December 2 lasted nine days; the sequence was gradual, not a single jump to televised confession.
claims.alternative: Mounting reporting, not a change of motive, explains the shift; any public figure under that pressure might do the same.

claims.claim: Author interpretation: the 2010 self-justification is Woods' post-treatment public account in treatment vocabulary; either way it frames his license in terms of results earned.
claims.passage: The self-justification needs more care: it is his account after treatment, read to a room, in treatment's words.
claims.inference: Achievement converted into personal license ('worked hard my entire life ... deserved') is the Three-specific part of the earning rule, even if treatment shaped the telling.
claims.alternative: The account may be the one therapy taught him to give rather than his 2009 reasoning; a One or Eight could voice entitlement too.

claims.claim: Author interpretation of the 2010 achievement-as-license logic as the Three-relevant use of the rule.
claims.passage: Woods' account turns results into a personal license: he had achieved, so he was owed. That is a Three's arithmetic, even if treatment shaped the telling.
claims.inference: For a One, deserving is moral and rules bind tighter; an Eight's appetite rarely needs a ledger. Converting achievement into license is closer to a Three's worth-through-performance.
claims.alternative: The distinction is typological interpretation, and the 2010 account is post-treatment (C98).

claims.claim: Woods married Elin Nordegren in 2004; they divorced in 2010.
claims.passage: He married Elin Nordegren in 2004; they divorced in 2010.
claims.inference: Orientation for the 2007-2010 section and the 2017 memoir quote.
claims.alternative: None material.

claims.claim: Woods ruptured his left ACL in July 2007 and played on it; after the 2008 Masters he chose a cleanup over reconstruction 'because I wanted to play the next three major championships', then suffered a double stress fracture of the left tibia preparing for the U.S. Open.
claims.passage: The knee came due in 2008. "I had ruptured my ACL in July the previous year, and I played on it with no ACL," he said a decade later. After the 2008 Masters he chose a cleanup over reconstruction: "'Well, we'll just do a cleanup job first,' because I wanted to play the next three major championships." Then came a double stress fracture in his left tibia
claims.inference: A ten-month choice to keep competing on a damaged knee, not a one-week discovery; corrects the draft's 'doctors found' framing.
claims.alternative: Recollection ten years later; competitive need explains it in any type.

claims.claim: No one outside Woods' inner circle knew he played the 2008 U.S. Open with the fracture; he announced it two days after the playoff.
claims.passage: No one outside his inner circle knew. He won after an 18-hole playoff and a sudden-death hole against Rocco Mediate. That scene is the Eight reading's best evidence, and it returns below. Two days later he announced the fracture: the ditch habit again, the injury kept out of sight until the result was in.
claims.inference: The 2008 episode contains concealment until the result was in, a foothold for the Three reading beside the Eight's defiance.
claims.alternative: Hiding an injury from rivals is ordinary competitive practice.

claims.claim: Woods' 1997-98 swing rebuild cost him: he struggled through 1998, winning just once.
claims.passage: The rebuild cost him: he struggled through 1998, winning just once
claims.inference: He accepted public under-performance to fix flaws he saw after a record win.
claims.alternative: Counterevidence for Three as much as evidence: a One's standard or a Five's mastery predicts it (C116).

claims.claim: By June 2004 Woods had parted with Harmon (August 2002), had not won a major since, and was reworking his swing; Harmon said Woods' repeated 'I am close, I feel really good about what I am doing' 'might be a bit of denial'.
claims.passage: By June 2004 he was doing it again: split from Harmon, reworking his swing, without a major since the split
claims.inference: A second self-imposed public slump for a swing change.
claims.alternative: Same as C103; Harmon is a former coach turned critic.

claims.claim: Harmon, by then a TV commentator, said in 2004 that Woods saying 'I am close, I feel really good about what I am doing' at every interview 'might be a bit of denial'.
claims.passage: Harmon's jab cut the same way: Woods telling every interviewer "I am close, I feel really good about what I am doing" "might be a bit of denial," he said
claims.inference: A coach describing Woods projecting success during a drought; read in the edit as bearing on image as much as on Eight directness.
claims.alternative: Hedged ('I think it might be') and from a former coach turned media critic with his own incentives.

claims.claim: Author interpretation: the 2004 face-to-face complaint reads both ways, Eight code or Three objection to public criticism.
claims.passage: It sounds like an Eight's code, but the complaint was that the criticism went public, which bothers a Three as much.
claims.inference: Removes the draft's 'textbook Eight line' overstatement.
claims.alternative: An Eight's loyalty code can include objecting to public betrayal.

claims.claim: Williams is a hostile witness: fired in 2011, he later made a racially charged remark about Woods at a caddie awards dinner, and had a book to sell; Woods' 2011 reply was 'I know he looks at it probably differently than I do. But, hey, life goes forward.'
claims.passage: Williams is a hostile witness: fired in 2011, he later made a racially charged remark about Woods at a caddie awards dinner, and he had a book to sell. Woods' reply in 2011: "I know he looks at it probably differently than I do. But, hey, life goes forward."
claims.inference: Gives the reader Williams' credibility limits and Woods' response beside the hostile claims.
claims.alternative: Williams' animus does not make his on-course account false.

claims.claim: After the 2021 crash Woods said it had been 'damn-near there if I was going to walk out of that hospital with one leg'.
claims.passage: he said it had been "damn-near there if I was going to walk out of that hospital with one leg."
claims.inference: Establishes the severity behind 'two legs' and the Everest remark.
claims.alternative: Self-report in a relayed interview; consistent with the medical record of open fractures (S72).

claims.claim: Woods made the cut at the April 2022 Masters about 14 months after the crash; withdrew from the 2023 Masters and had ankle fusion surgery in April 2023; ruptured his left Achilles in March 2025, at 49, while ramping up training.
claims.passage: He made the cut at the April 2022 Masters, about 14 months after the crash ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods)). In April 2023 he withdrew from the Masters and had ankle fusion surgery, and in March 2025, at 49, he ruptured his left Achilles tendon while ramping up his training
claims.inference: His behavior kept testing the 2021 'that's okay': repeated returns and training through injury echo the 2017 'need for competition'.
claims.alternative: Competitive need and identity explain returns in any type.

claims.claim: Woods' 2026 statement named no cause for the crash, and the court filing described the treatment only as an 'intensive, highly individualized and medically integrated program'.
claims.passage: Neither arrest is good type evidence. In 2017 he tied his to medication after back surgery; in 2026 his statement named no cause, and the court filing described the treatment only in general terms.
claims.inference: Replaces the draft's unsupported 'chronic pain' causal claim; neither arrest is counted as type evidence.
claims.alternative: Pain management and dependence are both possible; the article chooses neither.
claims.review_trigger: Re-check if Woods, his representatives or court records describe the cause of the 2026 crash or the nature of the treatment.

claims.claim: Author interpretation and type trigger: the 2026 retreat (stepping away, treatment abroad, declining the captaincy, no-questions appearance) looks as much like a Five's withdrawal as a Three's repair; a return, an open interview about the treatment or a quiet exit could move the 3-vs-5 reading.
claims.passage: By this profile's own test, the 2026 retreat looks as much like a Five's withdrawal as a Three's repair; a return, an open interview about the treatment or a quiet exit could move the reading.
claims.inference: The 2026 response is not counted as Three evidence.
claims.alternative: Legal and medical constraints, not motive, may explain the retreat.
claims.review_trigger: Re-test the Type 3 vs Type 5 call (and the medium confidence) when Woods gives an unscripted interview about the treatment, returns to competition, or formally retires from tour play.

claims.claim: Author interpretation: Six fits the father's-code loyalty and low trust but fails on doubt and authority-seeking (he overrode his doctors); Seven fits the 2009 temptations but not decades of painful practice.
claims.passage: A [Six](/enneagram-corner/enneagram-type-6), loyal to a father's code and slow to trust, fits the SEAL chapter below, but Sixes are marked by doubt and a search for trusted authority, and Woods answered his doctors with "Ah, I don't know about that." A Seven fits the temptations of 2009, not decades of hands-bleeding practice.
claims.inference: Tests the types the draft invoked or skipped (enneagram-06).
claims.alternative: A counterphobic Six can override authority; one sentence each is a light test.

claims.claim: The Tiger Slam was Woods' four consecutive major titles across 2000 and 2001.
claims.passage: The Tiger Slam was his four straight major titles in 2000 and 2001.
claims.inference: Orientation for Lavner's line.
claims.alternative: None material.

claims.claim: Woods' 15 majors rank second among men.
claims.passage: Only one man has won more majors.
claims.inference: Orientation on scale of achievement.
claims.alternative: None material.
claims.review_trigger: Re-check if Woods or another man wins a major that changes the ranking.

claims.claim: Author interpretation: Woods twice accepted lean public years to rebuild his swing (1998, by 2004), which a One's standard or a Five's mastery explains at least as well as a Three.
claims.passage: A Three is supposed to dodge visible failure, yet Woods accepted lean public years to rebuild his swing in 1998 and again by 2004, which a One's standard or a Five's mastery explains at least as well.
claims.inference: Counterevidence recorded in the type section (fan-03).
claims.alternative: A Three may accept short-term failure for a better long-term result.

claims.claim: Author interpretation: the earning rule itself is not type-specific (Earl taught it; common athlete ethic; One or Eight could hold it).
claims.passage: The rule itself proves little: Earl taught it, many athletes share it, and a One or an Eight could hold it as sincerely.
claims.inference: Labels the rule as the profile's organizing thread, not discriminator evidence (critic-02, enneagram-03).
claims.alternative: None; this is a limit statement.

claims.claim: Author interpretation: the 2008 episode gives the Three a foothold because the injury stayed hidden until he had won.
claims.passage: Even there the Three keeps a foothold, since he hid the injury until he had won, though hiding an injury from rivals is also plain competitive sense.
claims.inference: Acknowledges concealment in the Eight's best scene (fan-01).
claims.alternative: Concealment from competitors is standard practice.

claims.claim: Author interpretation: the Eight explains the 2008 U.S. Open better, and the temper and the aloofness after first meetings cut against a Three's polish; hence medium confidence.
claims.passage: The Eight explanation still answers the 2008 U.S. Open better, and the temper, along with the aloofness people report once a first meeting is over, cuts against a Three's usual polish. That is why confidence is medium.
claims.inference: Calibrates confidence.
claims.alternative: None; a limit statement.

type_hypothesis.against: Substantial observations resist Type 3. (1) The 2008 U.S. Open, overriding doctors and caddie (C06, C57, C58, C101), is better explained by an Eight; on-course temper he let show for years (C38, C73, C107) and the aloofness that follows first meetings (C60) cut against a Three's polish. (2) His first, least pressured response to exposure in December 2009 was a privacy boundary he said he would hold 'even though it's difficult' (C03, C129). (3) The crisis-era image repair is confounded: the 2007 trade is not shown to be Woods' own act (C04, C56) and the 2010 apology is what almost anyone with a marriage and business partners at stake would do (C80). (4) He twice accepted lean public years to rebuild his swing (C103, C104, C116), which a One's standard or a Five's mastery explains at least as well. (5) Friends describe a private introvert who wants to be left alone with a book (C12), and his privacy and secrecy fit a Five (C62); the 2026 retreat looks as much like Five withdrawal as Three repair (C111). (6) 'Core values', 'by my standard' and 'I expect more from myself' give a One reading some support, and a One under strain can grant himself an exemption (C94). (7) The earning rule itself is Earl's and a common athlete ethic, so its recurrence (C08, C10) is not type-specific (C117). (8) Being proclaimed 'the Chosen One' and on TV at two (C21, C25) is circumstance that could produce a performance-centred identity in any type.
type_hypothesis.alternative_case: Type 8 is the strongest alternative. It explains overriding his doctors and caddie to win the 2008 U.S. Open on a ruptured ACL and a double stress fracture (C06, C57, C58, C101), the self-imposed painful practice (C09), the face-to-face code with his old coach (C19, read both ways in C106), denial of vulnerability ('bottles things up', C17), the appetite of 2009 (C01; the Buddhist 'impulse' language is weak evidence, C37), the risk-seeking SEAL training (C16, C43), visible temper on the course (C38, C107), and a first response to exposure that held a boundary (C03, C129). Type 5 is a serious second: the introvert friends describe (C12), lifelong privacy and secrecy about his process (C62, C61), compartmentalization (C17), an adult and military childhood world with few peers (C82), low trust (C44), and a 2026 retreat that resembles withdrawal (C111). Type 1 is weaker but not ruled out (C94, C28). Six fits the father's-code loyalty but fails on doubt and authority-seeking; Seven fits 2009's temptations but not decades of grinding practice (C112).
type_hypothesis.discriminator: What a public humiliation does to him once it is over, observed where commercial incentive no longer predicts the answer. Six years after the 2010 apology, his friend Michael Jordan, via Wright Thompson, describes Woods as 'so haunted by his public shaming that he obsesses over it', 'Rabbit Ears' who 'hears everything', and a man who 'wants to erase the things that happened' (C95). An Eight usually stops caring what strangers think once the fight is over; a Five detaches from commentary; a One's torment is usually the inner critic over the wrong itself (C120, C130). Second, the 2010 self-account turns achievement into a personal license ('worked hard my entire life ... deserved ... entitled', C01, C98, C99): for a One deserving is moral and binds tighter, and an Eight's appetite rarely needs an earned ledger. The earning rule itself (C08, C10) is labeled non-specific (C117), and the 2007-2010 crisis sequence is treated as consistent with but not proof of a Three (C80, C129). Limits: C95 is one friend's account, partly paraphrased by one reporter, with Woods' camp declining comment, and rumination also fits a Six or plain shame; the 2010 account was prepared after 45 days of treatment (C98, C127). The Eight still answers the 2008 U.S. Open better (C119), so confidence stays medium. The type, confidence and alternatives are unchanged.)
type_hypothesis.unexplained: The Navy SEAL pursuit at his peak and in the months after his father's death (C16, C43): a dangerous, audience-less identity tied to Earl that cost him at the 2006 U.S. Open and has no golf payoff. The aloofness that sets in after a first meeting (C60) and the on-course temper he let damage his image (C38, C73, C107). His willingness to slump publicly for swing rebuilds (C116). The shift from 'no lessons' to Earl-style mental tests with his son (C24, C65). The 2017 and 2026 driving arrests (C29, C34, C66, C110): the 2017 one he tied to self-managed medication after surgery; the cause of the 2026 crash and the nature of the treatment are undisclosed, and neither is type evidence. The 2026 retreat (C111) is unresolved evidence for the 3-vs-5 balance.
